# An explicit domain-preserving projection scheme for scalar stochastic differential equations
###### Abstract
We develop an explicit domain-preserving projection scheme for scalar stochastic differential equations whose solutions evolve in a prescribed interval. A Lamperti-type transformation converts the original equation into one with additive noise, whose drift may be singular near finite boundaries or grow polynomially at infinity. The proposed domain-preserving projected Euler–Maruyama (DPPEM) scheme combines an explicit Euler–Maruyama step with projection onto a step-size-dependent interior interval.
Their schemes first project the current approximation onto a ball whose radius increases as the step size decreases and then perform the update using the projected state. For additive noise, their results yield strong order one convergence of the projected EM scheme Beyn et al. [2017]. These results assume coefficients defined on ℝ^d and do not directly cover drifts singular at finite interval endpoints. Interval problems thus require additional control near finite boundaries and, when the domain is unbounded, at infinity.
To account for drift singularities near finite endpoints and polynomial growth at infinity, we propose a fully explicit DPPEM scheme and provide a unified analysis of its strong convergence. Consider the scalar SDE

Like many mathematical subjects, we must first introduce some terminology and notation before we can get to the “fun stuff.” Mathematicians distinguish between vector and scalar (pronounced “SKAY-lur”) quantities. You’re already an expert on scalars—scalar is the technical term for an ordinary number. We use this term specifically when we wish to emphasize that a particular quantity is not a vector quantity. For example, as we will discuss shortly, “velocity” and “displacement” are vector quantities, whereas “speed” and “distance” are scalar quantities. The dimension of a vector tells how many numbers the vector contains. Vectors may be of any positive dimension, including one. In fact, a scalar can be considered a 1D vector. context.snippet: AN EXPLICIT DOMAIN-PRESERVING PROJECTED MILSTEIN SCHEME WITH STRONG ORDER ONE FOR STOCHASTIC SYSTEMS XINGWEI HU1,2, YAOZHONG HU2, AND AIGUO XIAO1,3,* Abstract. A variety of domain-preserving numerical schemes have been developed for scalar stochastic differ- ential equations and for several classes of multidimensional systems, including those defined on hyperrectangles and positive orthants. To accommodate more general domain constraints, we consider stochastic systems on bounded or unbounded open convex polyhedral domains, where coefficients may exhibit boundary singularities and polynomial growth. Under local regularity, growth and boundary assumptions, we establish well-posedness and integrability estimates for the exact solution. Then we construct an explicit projected Milstein scheme that preserves the domain by applying a Euclidean projection onto a step-size-dependent interior set after each Milstein update. For systems driven by multidimensional commutative noise, we prove strong order-one convergence for the maximum grid error in Lp, for suitable p > 1 and sufficiently small step sizes under addi- tional weighted regularity and stability conditions. The proof combines these integrability estimates with local Milstein consistency, localization and weighted stability, without requiring a priori step-size-uniform moment or boundary inverse-moment bounds for the numerical approximation. Applications to constrained stochastic models and numerical experiments illustrate the observed first-order convergence behavior. 1. In this work, we propose high-order boundary-preserving numerical schemes for the strong approximation for some scalar stochastic differential equations with invariant do- mains being open and bounded intervals. The proposed methods involve using the Lamperti transform to map the SDE to another SDE with additive noise with a trivial invariant do- main. Then, by imposing regularity assumptions on the original coefficient functions, we can guarantee that the drift coefficient function of the transformed SDE is regular, and known high-order schemes can be used to achieve the desired convergence order. ###### Abstract

We develop an explicit domain-preserving projection scheme for scalar stochastic differential equations whose solutions evolve in a prescribed interval. A Lamperti-type transformation converts the original equation into one with additive noise, whose drift may be singular near finite boundaries or grow polynomially at infinity. The proposed domain-preserving projected Euler–Maruyama (DPPEM) scheme combines an explicit Euler–Maruyama step with projection onto a step-size-dependent interior interval. Under one-sided Lipschitz, boundary, and weighted growth assumptions, with projection parameters chosen according to the coefficient growth and available moment orders, we establish strong order one convergence for admissible moment orders. The analysis combines local consistency and stability estimates with moment and boundary negative moment bounds for the exact solution. Numerical moment bounds follow from the convergence estimate, while numerical negative moment bounds are obtained under additional conditions. Estimates for the inverse Lamperti map yield strong order one convergence for the original equations in the CIR, Heston 3/2, CEV, Aït–Sahalia, and bounded interest-rate models under the stated model conditions. Numerical experiments illustrate the predicted convergence rates and compare computational costs with the Lamperti backward Euler–Maruyama scheme.

On the other hand, another kind of approaches to achieve this goal are the projection methods, which we will apply to preserve the conserved quantity in the stochastic case.

The basic idea of projection methods is to combine an arbitrary one-step approximation $\widehat{X}_{t,x}$ starting at $x$ together with a projection $P$ onto the invariant submanifold $\mathcal{M}_{x}$ in every step. Thus the procedures of the methods at each step are:

1. Compute the one-step approximation $\widehat{X}_{t,x}$.
2. Compute $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, for $\bar{X}_{t,x}=\widehat{X}_{t,x}+\Phi\lambda$ s.t. $I(\bar{X}_{t,x})=I(x)$.

Here the vector $\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ defines the direction of the projection, and $\lambda$ is a scalar chosen such that the new approximation $\bar{X}_{t,x}$ belongs to the invariant submanifold $\mathcal{M}_{x}$ properly. The general idea of the procedures is shown in Fig. 1.

Figure 1: Basic idea of the projection methods.

In fact the projection direction $\Phi$ is not unique here, and the standard orthogonal projection chooses $\nabla I(\bar{X}_{t,x})$ as $\Phi(x,\bar{X}_{t,x})$ [7, Chap. IV]. In order to reduce computational cost we just use $\nabla I(\widehat{X}_{t,x})$ or $\nabla I(x)$ to replace $\nabla I(\bar{X}_{t,x})$. So we combine the relationship and get $\bar{X}_{t,x}$ above by solving a non-linear equation with respect to $\lambda$. In fact, we find that $\lambda$ approaches 0 at each step, so we just set $\lambda_{0}=0$ in Newton iteration to solve it.

###### Abstract

We develop an explicit domain-preserving projection scheme for scalar stochastic differential equations whose solutions evolve in a prescribed interval. A Lamperti-type transformation converts the original equation into one with additive noise, whose drift may be singular near finite boundaries or grow polynomially at infinity. The proposed domain-preserving projected Euler–Maruyama (DPPEM) scheme combines an explicit Euler–Maruyama step with projection onto a step-size-dependent interior interval. Under one-sided Lipschitz, boundary, and weighted growth assumptions, with projection parameters chosen according to the coefficient growth and available moment orders, we establish strong order one convergence for admissible moment orders. The analysis combines local consistency and stability estimates with moment and boundary negative moment bounds for the exact solution. Numerical moment bounds follow from the convergence estimate, while numerical negative moment bounds are obtained under additional conditions. Estimates for the inverse Lamperti map yield strong order one convergence for the original equations in the CIR, Heston 3/2, CEV, Aït–Sahalia, and bounded interest-rate models under the stated model conditions. Numerical experiments illustrate the predicted convergence rates and compare computational costs with the Lamperti backward Euler–Maruyama scheme.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12630303/)Abstract

In Armstrong et al. (Proc Lond Math Soc (3) 119(1):176–213, 2019) the authors define three projections of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$-valued stochastic differential equations (SDEs) onto submanifolds: the Stratonovich, Itô-vector and Itô-jet projections. In this paper, after a brief survey of SDEs on manifolds, we begin by giving these projections a natural, coordinate-free description, each in terms of a specific representation of manifold-valued SDEs. We use these to show that the Itô-vector and Itô-jet projections satisfy respectively a weak and mean-square optimality criterion “for small t”: this is achieved by solving constrained optimisation problems. These results confirm, but do not rely on the approach taken in Armstrong et al. (Proc Lond Math Soc (3) 119(1):176–213, 2019), which is formulated in terms of weak and strong Itô–Taylor expansions. In the final section we exhibit examples showing how the three projections can differ, and explore alternative notions of optimality.

keenable.snippet:
Flow-based and diffusion-based models have become the principal means of learning and sampling high-dimensional probability distributions, from images and video to proteins, molecules and physical fields, and increasingly language. Each carries a simple law to the law of the data along a curve of probability measures, and behind the variety of their names lie three geometries, those of the state space on which the data live, of the space of probability measures through which the curve passes, and of the space of paths traced by the generating process. A single analytic idea runs through the subject. Every score identity used to train a diffusion model is an integration by parts, on the noise, on the data or on Wiener space, and Malliavin calculus extends this to nonlinear and infinite-dimensional diffusions. We develop these foundations with full definitions and follow them through normalising flows, flow matching and few-step maps, diffusion models and their convergence theory, conditioning, Schrödinger bridges and stochastic control, and their extension to manifolds, Lie groups, discrete and function spaces and jump processes.

keenable.title: A fast automatically adaptive integral equation solver for nonlinear two-point boundary value systems
keenable.snippet: We present a fast, high-order, automatically adaptive integral-equation solver for nonlinear two-point boundary value systems. The method builds on the fast direct solver for linear second-kind integral equations and completes the mathematical formulation needed for general boundary conditions, including cases in which the simplest background Green’s function is singular and cases with genuinely rank-deficient boundary conditions. Nonlinear problems are written as nonlinear second-kind integral equations and are solved by combining this fast adaptive linear solver with Newton iteration and user-specified continuation. In this way the nonlinear solver inherits the full strengths of the linear integral-equation method: a fast direct solver, arbitrary order accuracy, and automatic adaptive resolution with only a small overhead over a solve on the final mesh. The resulting algorithm is particularly effective for problems with localized or multiscale structure, including boundary layers, dense oscillations, transition regions, hypersensitive optimal-control systems, and singular perturbations. The same framework also provides a computational foundation for future studies of bifurcation and solution-branch exploration.

keenable.snippet: We analyze a fully discrete finite element projection method for the stochastic incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and multiplicative noise. keenable.title: Elliptic regularization for anisotropic mean curvature flow
keenable.snippet: We develop an elliptic regularization scheme for anisotropic mean curvature flow in arbitrary dimension, with general norms serving as surface tension and mobility. Starting from a non-fattening set of finite perimeter, we prove that the vertically rescaled minimizers and translating solitons converge in the Kuratowski sense to the unique generalized level-set motion, and locally in BV to the flat flow. Furthermore, by implementing a restarting and matching procedure prior to curvature identification, we establish for the limit flat flow a coupled phase-transport and surface-energy dissipation balance valid for arbitrary, possibly crystalline, anisotropies. When the surface tension is continuously differentiable (away from the origin) and strictly convex, we further prove that the flat flow is a BV flow and that its reduced boundary defines a unit-density anisotropic Brakke flow. To our knowledge, this is the first construction of unit-density anisotropic Brakke flows valid for every strictly convex differentiable surface tension, in arbitrary dimension and for prescribed non-fattening initial data, without assuming perimeter convergence.

# An explicit domain-preserving projection scheme for scalar stochastic differential equations  
###### Abstract  
We develop an explicit domain-preserving projection scheme for scalar stochastic differential equations whose solutions evolve in a prescribed interval. A Lamperti-type transformation converts the original equation into one with additive noise, whose drift may be singular near finite boundaries or grow polynomially at infinity. The proposed domain-preserving projected Euler–Maruyama (DPPEM) scheme combines an explicit Euler–Maruyama step with projection onto a step-size-dependent interior interval. Under one-sided Lipschitz, boundary, and weighted growth assumptions, with projection parameters chosen according to the coefficient growth and available moment orders, we establish strong order one convergence for admissible moment orders. The analysis combines local consistency and stability estimates with moment and boundary negative moment bounds for the exact solution. Numerical moment bounds follow from the convergence estimate, while numerical negative moment bounds are obtained under additional conditions. Estimates for the inverse Lamperti map yield strong order one convergence for the original equations in the CIR, Heston 3/2, CEV, Aït–Sahalia, and bounded interest-rate models under the stated model conditions. Numerical experiments illustrate the predicted convergence rates and compare computational costs with the Lamperti backward Euler–Maruyama scheme.

In this blog, we will explore the theory behind SDEs, understand why numerical methods are necessary, derive the Euler-Maruyama scheme step by step, discuss its convergence properties, walk through a practical implementation, and examine its strengths, limitations, and alternatives. By the end, you should have a solid conceptual and practical understanding of how to numerically solve SDEs using this foundational method.
## Understanding Stochastic Differential Equations  
### General Form of an SDE  
A general scalar SDE can be written as:  
$$ dX\_t = a(X\_t, t),dt + b(X\_t, t),dW\_t $$  
Here, $X\_t$ represents the state of the system at time $t$, $a(X\_t, t)$ is called the **drift coefficient**, and $b(X\_t, t)$ is called the **diffusion coefficient**. The term $dW\_t$ represents an infinitesimal increment of a Wiener process (also known as Brownian motion), which introduces the stochastic component into the equation.  
The drift term $a(X\_t, t),dt$ behaves much like the right-hand side of an ordinary differential equation — it describes the deterministic tendency of the system. The diffusion term $b(X\_t, t),dW\_t$, on the other hand, injects randomness proportional to the magnitude of $b(X\_t, t)$. When $b(X\_t, t) = 0$, the SDE reduces to an ordinary differential equation.

Just as with ODE solvers, stability is a concern for SDE solvers. For certain SDEs — particularly those with strong mean-reverting dynamics or stiff drift terms — the Euler-Maruyama method can become numerically unstable for larger step sizes, producing wildly oscillating or diverging trajectories even when the true solution remains bounded.  
Additionally, as mentioned earlier, the method does not preserve qualitative properties of the solution such as positivity or boundedness. In this work, we consider scalar stochastic differential equations (SDEs) whose solutions remain
within a bounded domain for all time. Such a domain is called an invariant domain: whenever the
initial condition belongs to the domain, the corresponding solution remains in the domain for all later
times. We propose numerical schemes that preserve this invariant domain and achieve arbitrarily high
strong convergence order, provided that the coefficients of the SDE are sufficiently regular. Examples
of such SDEs include, but are not limited to, Allen–Cahn type SDEs, SIS-type SDEs, and Nagumo-

###### Abstract

We develop an explicit domain-preserving projection scheme for scalar stochastic differential equations whose solutions evolve in a prescribed interval. A Lamperti-type transformation converts the original equation into one with additive noise, whose drift may be singular near finite boundaries or grow polynomially at infinity. The proposed domain-preserving projected Euler–Maruyama (DPPEM) scheme combines an explicit Euler–Maruyama step with projection onto a step-size-dependent interior interval. Under one-sided Lipschitz, boundary, and weighted growth assumptions, with projection parameters chosen according to the coefficient growth and available moment orders, we establish strong order one convergence for admissible moment orders. The analysis combines local consistency and stability estimates with moment and boundary negative moment bounds for the exact solution. A scalar diffusion model on \(X_t>0\) can be written \(dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t)\,dW_t\), where \(W_t\) is standard Brownian motion. When \(\sigma\) depends on \(X_t\), a fixed-size increment of Brownian noise produces different-sized state changes at different concentrations. The Lamperti transform changes coordinates so that the transformed diffusion coefficient is constant. This can simplify analysis and simulation, but it does not remove the original model’s boundary behavior.
The key is to keep track of the transformed state space. A boundary at zero might map to a finite endpoint, to minus infinity, or to a coordinate where the transformed drift is singular. The transformed equation is valid in the interior; it does not, by itself, specify what to do when a numerical step reaches or crosses an endpoint.

## From Ordinary Calculus to Stochastic Calculus: What Changes?

Everything in this calculus series so far has rested on one quiet assumption: that the thing you are differentiating is *smooth*. Zoom in far enough on a smooth curve and it looks like a straight line. That is the entire content of the derivative from first principles, and it is why Taylor expansions work: the leftover curvature shrinks faster than the step, so you can throw it away.

## Transforming State Variables in SDEs

A stochastic differential equation describes one quantity, but nothing forces you to simulate, price or analyse it in the coordinates it was written in. A commodity price can be studied through its logarithm, a short rate through its square root, an exchange rate through its reciprocal. This article is about the general machinery of that choice: how the drift and diffusion change when you move from X to Y = f(X), why quants make the move, and the point most textbooks skip. **Changing coordinates changes the numerical scheme.** Euler on X and Euler on f(X) are two different algorithms with two different errors, and the one that looks cleaner is not automatically the more accurate one. ## 1. Why Change the State Variable at All

Every SDE model comes with a natural variable: the price, the rate, the spread. That variable is chosen because it is what the market quotes, not because it is convenient to compute with. A change of state variable keeps the same random world (the same paths, the same probabilities) and only relabels the number you track along each path. - **Constant noise.** If the diffusion coefficient depends on the state, a transform can make it identically one. This is the Lamperti transform, and it makes the noise additive, which helps estimation, simulation and proofs.

## Explicit Time-Stepping for PDEs

Every finite-difference pricer has to answer one question before it computes anything: once you have discretised the option value on a grid of stock prices, how do you march that grid backwards through time? The simplest answer is the explicit scheme — forward Euler in the time variable. Each new row of the grid is written down directly from the row you already have. There is no matrix to factorise, no system to solve, and the whole method fits in a dozen lines of code.

That simplicity is real, and it is why explicit stepping is the first scheme anyone writes. It is also why the scheme has a hard constraint attached: it only works if your time step is small enough. This article is about that constraint — where it comes from, what it looks like for Black-Scholes specifically, and why the most commonly shipped version of the formula is wrong in a way that can make a catastrophically large time step look perfectly safe.

**∂V/∂t + ½σ²S² ∂²V/∂S² + rS ∂V/∂S − rV = 0**

We know the solution at one instant — at maturity, where *V* is just the payoff — and we want it at today's date. So we solve backwards. It is conventional to substitute τ = *T* − *t*, the time remaining, which turns the problem into a forward march in τ starting from the payoff. Flow-based and diffusion-based models have become the principal means of learning and sampling high-dimensional probability distributions, from images and video to proteins, molecules and physical fields, and increasingly language. Each carries a simple law to the law of the data along a curve of probability measures, and behind the variety of their names lie three geometries, those of the state space on which the data live, of the space of probability measures through which the curve passes, and of the space of paths traced by the generating process. ultimate.title: A fast automatically adaptive integral equation solver for nonlinear two-point boundary value systems
ultimate.snippet: We present a fast, high-order, automatically adaptive integral-equation solver for nonlinear two-point boundary value systems. The method builds on the fast direct solver for linear second-kind integral equations and completes the mathematical formulation needed for general boundary conditions, including cases in which the simplest background Green’s function is singular and cases with genuinely rank-deficient boundary conditions. Nonlinear problems are written as nonlinear second-kind integral equations and are solved by combining this fast adaptive linear solver with Newton iteration and user-specified continuation. The resulting algorithm is particularly effective for problems with localized or multiscale structure, including boundary layers, dense oscillations, transition regions, hypersensitive optimal-control systems, and singular perturbations. The same framework also provides a computational foundation for future studies of bifurcation and solution-branch exploration.
